title: Moving from Kenya to the USA: Complete Guide
excerpt: Visa options, paperwork, and what to expect in your first few months, a practical roadmap for Kenyans relocating to the US.

content: Relocating from Kenya to the United States is a process that unfolds in stages, from choosing the right visa category, to gathering documents, to the months after you land when everyday life still feels unfamiliar. This guide walks through what that path actually looks like, drawing on the official process laid out by the U.S. government, so you can plan with fewer surprises.

Most Kenyans move to the US through one of three main routes: a family-sponsored petition filed by a relative who is a US citizen or permanent resident, an employment-based visa sponsored by a US employer, or the Diversity Visa Lottery, which randomly selects a limited number of applicants from countries with historically low immigration to the US each year. Each category has its own eligibility rules, processing timelines, and paperwork, so the first real decision is figuring out which one actually applies to your situation.
The official process runs through USCIS and the

content: , which covers petition filing, National Visa Center (NVC) processing, and your consular interview step by step. Reading through that process before you start collecting documents will save you from redoing paperwork later, since requirements differ slightly depending on your visa category.

Regardless of category, expect to assemble a similar core set of documents: a valid passport, birth certificate, police clearance certificates from every country you've lived in for an extended period, medical exam results from an approved panel physician, and financial evidence showing you or your sponsor can support yourself once you arrive. For family and employment petitions, you'll also need the original approval notice (Form I-797) once USCIS approves the underlying petition.

Small mistakes, like a name that doesn't match exactly across documents, or a police clearance that's expired by the time of your interview, are some of the most common reasons cases stall. Start gathering paperwork as early as possible and keep certified translations ready for anything not already in English.

body.text: What the Timeline Actually Looks Like

content: Once your petition is approved, budget several months for NVC processing and background checks before your consular interview is even scheduled. Family-based cases can take longer than employment-based ones depending on the specific category and visa bulletin movement, since demand in some family categories exceeds the annual number of visas available. Check current visa bulletin dates and processing times directly on
before making any firm travel or moving plans, since timelines shift from month to month.

Once your interview is approved, you'll typically receive your visa within a couple of weeks, at which point you have a limited window to actually enter the US before the visa expires. This is the point where booking flights, arranging temporary housing, and shipping belongings all need to come together quickly.

body.text: Settling In: The First Few Months

content: After you land, the early priorities are usually the same regardless of visa category: applying for a Social Security number, opening a US bank account, finding housing, and figuring out health insurance. Many new arrivals underestimate how long it takes for a Social Security card to arrive by mail, which can delay everything from a lease application to a phone plan, so it helps to apply as soon as you're eligible.

title: How Kenyans Abroad Can Send Money Home Cheaply
excerpt: Comparing transfer fees, exchange rates, and delivery speed across the services Kenyans in the diaspora use most.

content: For most Kenyans in the diaspora, sending money home isn't a one-time event, it's a recurring part of life, whether that's supporting parents, paying school fees, or helping with a family project. Because it happens so often, even a small difference in fees or exchange rates adds up fast over a year. Here's how to think about the main options.

Transfer fees and exchange rate markups can quietly eat 3 to 8 percent of every remittance, depending on the provider and the payment method you use. That markup is often hidden inside the exchange rate itself rather than shown as a separate fee, which makes it easy to underestimate how much you're actually paying. Two providers advertising the same flat fee can still cost very differently once you account for the rate they use to convert dollars to shillings.
Services like

publish their fees upfront and use the real mid-market exchange rate, which usually makes them cheaper for bank-to-M-Pesa transfers than a traditional wire from a US bank. The tradeoff is that transfers can take a bit longer to land compared to services built specifically for instant cash pickup.

is worth comparing too, especially for cash pickup in areas without reliable mobile money access, or when you need funds to arrive within minutes rather than a day. Its network of physical agent locations across Kenya is one of its biggest advantages, even if the exchange rate isn't always the most competitive.

A traditional international wire from a US bank is usually the slowest and most expensive route, often layering a flat fee on top of a weaker exchange rate, plus a possible receiving fee on the Kenyan side. Services that deposit directly into M-Pesa tend to be faster and cheaper for smaller, more frequent transfers, since the money is usable almost immediately without a trip to a bank branch.

body.text: Tips to Cut Costs Every Time

content: Compare the total amount the recipient actually gets, not just the advertised fee, since that's the only number that reflects the real exchange rate markup. Sending larger amounts less frequently, rather than many small transfers, also reduces how much you lose to flat fees over time. title: Best Time to Fly from the USA to Kenya
excerpt: Seasonal pricing patterns, layover routes, and how to time your trip home around the holidays without overpaying.

content: Flying between the US and Kenya is a long haul no matter which route you take, so getting the timing and routing right makes a real difference, both in cost and in how the trip actually feels. Here's how to think about when to book and which route to take.

Fares from the US to Nairobi swing hardest around December and August, when diaspora travel peaks for the holidays and school breaks. That's also when Kenyan schools are on their longer holidays, so families traveling together tend to cluster around the same weeks, pushing prices up well before departure. If your travel dates are flexible, shifting by even a week or two outside these windows can mean a noticeably lower fare.
Tracking prices for a few weeks on

before booking usually surfaces the cheaper travel windows, since it shows how fares move across nearby dates rather than locking you into a single search. Booking a couple of months ahead generally beats booking last minute for this route, especially around the December peak when seats fill up early.
For direct options, check

, which flies nonstop from New York JFK to Nairobi and connects to most other major Kenyan diaspora hubs through partner airlines. A one-stop itinerary through Europe or the Gulf is often cheaper than the direct route, but adds several hours to total travel time, so it's a real tradeoff between cost and how long you're actually in transit.

Long-haul flights to Nairobi mean checked-bag allowances matter more than usual, especially if you're bringing gifts or supplies for family, so check your airline's baggage policy before you pack rather than at the counter. title: Where to Buy Kenyan Food Abroad
excerpt: From sukuma wiki to Royco, here's where the diaspora finds a taste of home, plus a few online grocers worth bookmarking.

content: One of the first things most Kenyans abroad look for is a reliable source of home ingredients, things like Royco, Ketepa tea, maize flour, and the specific spices that make a dish taste right. The good news is that between dedicated online grocers, local African markets, and a bit of substitution know-how, most of it is easier to find than people expect.

ships pantry staples like Ketepa tea, Royco, and maize flour across the US, with curbside pickup available at select locations for diaspora communities near their stores. Ordering online is especially useful if you're not near a city with a large Kenyan or East African community, since it saves the drive and the guesswork of which local store might carry what you need.

is another reliable option, carrying Kenyan snacks, spices, and beauty products with fast shipping nationwide. Between the two, most staple ingredients for everyday Kenyan cooking are covered without needing a special trip, and both are worth comparing on shipping cost if you're stocking up in bulk rather than ordering small amounts often.

If you live near a larger metro area, a local African or Caribbean grocery store often carries overlapping staples like plantains, cassava flour, and spices used across East African cooking, even if it's not Kenyan-specific. These stores are also usually the best place to find fresh sukuma wiki or similar greens, which don't ship well and are best bought fresh and local rather than ordered online.

It's worth asking around in local Kenyan diaspora WhatsApp or Facebook groups too, since community members often know exactly which nearby store restocks specific items, or run informal group orders for things like fresh milk products or ingredients that are hard to find any other way.

body.text: What to Stock Up On When You Find a Good Source

content: Dry goods and shelf-stable items are the easiest to stock up on in bulk: Royco, Ketepa or other Kenyan teas, maize and millet flour, dried beans, and spice blends all keep well and are worth ordering in larger quantities to cut down on shipping costs per item. Fresh produce and dairy are the opposite, buy those locally and only in amounts you'll actually use before they spoil.

body.text: Cooking Kenyan Food With What's Available

content: When a specific ingredient isn't available even online, most Kenyan dishes tolerate reasonable substitutions, collard greens or kale can stand in for sukuma wiki, and any good all-purpose maize flour works for ugali even if it isn't a Kenyan brand. Knowing which substitutions actually hold up in a dish, versus which ones change it too much, comes with a bit of trial and error, but it means a missing ingredient rarely has to mean skipping a meal you're craving.

title: Buying Land in Kenya While Living Abroad
excerpt: How to vet a title deed, avoid common fraud schemes, and close a land purchase in Kenya from overseas.

content: Buying land in Kenya from overseas is one of the most common ways the diaspora invests back home, and also one of the easiest ways to lose money if you skip the verification steps. Distance makes it harder to spot red flags in person, so the process has to lean more heavily on documentation and trusted people on the ground.
Every land purchase in Kenya should start with a search on

, the Ministry of Lands' digital platform for title searches, transfers, and stamp duty. It's the fastest way to confirm a title deed is genuine, who actually owns the parcel, and whether there are any existing charges or disputes registered against it, before you send a single shilling as a deposit.

body.text: Common Land Fraud Schemes to Avoid

content: The most common schemes involve a seller who isn't actually the registered owner, forged title documents, or the same parcel being sold to multiple buyers before any transfer is finalized. Distance makes diaspora buyers a frequent target, since fraudsters count on you not being able to easily visit the site or the lands office in person to double-check what you're being told.
For disputes or historical land injustices, the
is the constitutional body with oversight of public land, and a useful resource if a deal looks even slightly irregular or if you need to research a parcel's history before committing.

body.text: Working With a Lawyer and Power of Attorney

content: A local lawyer who isn't connected to the seller or agent is worth the cost, since they can independently verify the title, draft the sale agreement, and confirm the transfer is properly registered. If you can't be physically present for signing, a power of attorney lets a trusted representative act on your behalf, but it should be drafted specifically for the transaction rather than left open-ended, to limit what it actually authorizes.
Buying from abroad usually means moving a large sum at once, so it pays to revisit our guide on

before you wire funds for a deposit or full payment, since the fees and exchange rate on a large transfer add up quickly. Only release full payment once the transfer is confirmed registered under your name, not simply once the seller says it's done.
